lesson.title: Teaching modelling and assessing it
lesson.subtitle: From a messy brief to a model you can defend

video.title: Teaching modelling and assessing it: From a messy brief to a model you can defend
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.

Prof Farah - head of department, Amman
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to a university lecturer (warm, collegial, precise)

scenes.narration: A student team's model of the campus shuttle cut cost by thirty percent. The transport office rejected it at once: it left the night students with no bus. The solver was right. The model was not. Why?
Today: why formulating a model is the hardest skill in optimisation, how to teach the modelling cycle, and how to assess models rather than just answers.

An optimisation model has decision variables, an objective and constraints. Choosing them is a judgement about the real problem. A missing constraint lets the solver exploit a loophole, just as a missing rule lets an agent game its reward.

Modelling is a cycle, not a single step. Understand the problem with stakeholders, formulate, solve, then validate the solution against reality. When validation fails, as with the night buses, return and revise.
The fix is one line: every route must have at least one bus in every time period with demand. With it, the cost saving drops to eighteen percent, and the office accepts the model.
Textbook exercises hand students the variables. Real work starts from a vague brief. Give students a short messy brief and a stakeholder to interview, and make them state every assumption.

If you grade only the optimal value, students learn to chase numbers. Grade the formulation, the stated assumptions, validation against the brief, and a sensitivity analysis. A short oral defence shows who understands the model.
Quick check! The solver found the true optimum of the students' model, yet the plan was rejected. Which stage of the modelling cycle failed?
Formulation: a real requirement was left out. Validation with the transport office caught it, and the cycle sent the team back to revise.
In the app, open the modeller lab. Turn a short brief into variables, an objective and constraints, solve it, and check the answer against the brief.
Your turn. Two teams report the same optimal cost. What best shows which team modelled the problem well?

Their stated assumptions, validation against the brief, and how they defend the model orally. Remember: modelling is a cycle, validation catches missing constraints, and assessment should reward the model, not just the number.

checkpoints.prompt: The solver found the true optimum, yet the plan was rejected. Which stage failed?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: a real requirement was missing from the model.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: the solver did its job; the model left out a constraint.

checkpoints.prompt: Two teams report the same optimal cost. What best shows who modelled well?

options.text: Assumptions, validation and an oral defence

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: the model and its justification, not the number.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: identical numbers can hide very different models.
